questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 9 explains how an opioid overdose progresses to cardiac arrest. Which mechanism does the manual describe?

answers.text: Opioids stimulate the heart to beat too fast
Opioids block oxygen absorption directly in the lungs
Opioids affect the brainstem and suppress the brain's natural drive to breathe, causing respiratory depression and slowing the heart rate
Opioids damage the kidneys, leading to immediate cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Opioids slow rather than stimulate the heart, primarily through respiratory depression and resulting hypoxia.
explanations.b: Opioids do not block oxygen absorption in the lungs; the failure is in the central drive to breathe.
explanations.c: AHA Part 9 says opioids affect the brainstem, which controls breathing; high doses suppress the natural drive to breathe, slow the heart rate, and can lead to cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Kidney damage is not the AHA-described mechanism by which opioid overdose causes cardiac arrest.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: An adult is unresponsive with slow, shallow breathing after a suspected drug exposure, and naloxone is available. AHA Part 9 makes a key safety point about giving naloxone in this situation. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Naloxone should be withheld unless the rescuer is sure of the drug taken
Naloxone reverses all known overdoses regardless of the substance
Naloxone is safe to administer even if you're not sure what drug the person took
Naloxone is reserved for ALS-only administration

explanations.a: Withholding naloxone while diagnostic certainty is sought delays reversal and worsens outcome.
explanations.b: Naloxone specifically reverses opioid effects; it does not reverse all overdoses.
explanations.c: AHA Part 9 explicitly says naloxone is safe to administer even if you are not sure what drug the person took.
explanations.d: Naloxone is widely available without a prescription in the United States and Canada and can be administered by lay rescuers.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 9 names two opioid antagonists currently available for reversal of opioid overdose in the United States. Which statement matches the manual?

answers.text: Atropine and epinephrine are the standard opioid antagonists
Only nalmefene is approved for opioid reversal
Only naloxone is an opioid antagonist; no other antagonist exists
Naloxone and nalmefene are both available; published clinical data are more robust for naloxone

explanations.a: Atropine and epinephrine are not opioid antagonists; they are used for different cardiac and resuscitation indications.
explanations.b: Naloxone is the more widely used and studied of the two; nalmefene is also available but is by prescription only as an intranasal product.
explanations.c: Multiple opioid antagonists exist; naloxone is the most common but not the only one.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9 names naloxone and nalmefene as the two opioid antagonists available, noting that to date, the published clinical data are more robust for naloxone.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: Per AHA Part 9, naloxone may be administered by which routes during an opioid emergency response by appropriately trained rescuers?

answers.text: Only via a deep subcutaneous injection in the abdomen
Only by mouth (oral)
Only as a continuous IV infusion
Intravenously, intramuscularly, and intranasally

explanations.a: Subcutaneous abdominal injection is not the AHA-recommended route for naloxone in opioid emergencies.
explanations.b: Oral naloxone is destroyed by first-pass metabolism and is not used for opioid reversal.
explanations.c: BLS naloxone is given as a single dose via standard routes, not as a continuous IV infusion.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9 lists intravenous, intramuscular, and intranasal as common routes for naloxone administration.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: After giving an initial dose of naloxone to an adult in suspected opioid overdose, the person does not respond. According to AHA Part 9, what is the recommended interval before considering a second dose?

answers.text: Wait at least 30 minutes before any second dose
Never give a second dose under any circumstances
Give a second dose if the person does not respond within 2 to 3 minutes after the first dose
Give 5 doses immediately one after another

explanations.a: Thirty minutes is too long given the potency of opioids and the risk of continued respiratory depression.
explanations.b: A second dose is sometimes necessary; never giving one is not the AHA position.
explanations.c: AHA Part 9 says given the potency of opiates, you may need to give a second dose of naloxone if the person does not respond within 2 to 3 minutes after the first dose.
explanations.d: Stacking 5 immediate doses is not the AHA recommendation; spaced doses based on response are appropriate.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 9 describes naloxone autoinjectors as a delivery method for opioid reversal. How does the manual characterize their action?

answers.text: Autoinjectors deliver oral tablets through a spring mechanism
Autoinjectors deliver a continuous intravenous infusion
Autoinjectors deliver naloxone via the eye
Naloxone handheld autoinjectors deliver a single dose via an intramuscular injection

explanations.a: Naloxone is not delivered as oral tablets via autoinjector; it is delivered intramuscularly.
explanations.b: Autoinjectors are not infusion devices; they deliver a single fixed dose.
explanations.c: Eye administration is not used for naloxone delivery.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9 says naloxone handheld autoinjectors deliver a single dose via an intramuscular injection.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 lists possible signs of heart attack beyond chest pain. Which set of locations matches what the manual describes for upper-body discomfort?

answers.text: Pain or discomfort that may occur in the left arm (commonly), both arms, upper back, neck, jaw, or stomach
Pain only in the right ankle
Pain only in the lower back below the waist
Pain only in the toes and feet

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 describes upper-body discomfort that can include the left arm — commonly — but can also occur in both arms, the upper back, neck, jaw, or stomach.
explanations.b: Right ankle pain is not on the AHA list of heart attack symptoms.
explanations.c: Isolated lower back pain below the waist is not the AHA-listed pattern.
explanations.d: Foot and toe pain are not on the AHA list of heart attack symptoms.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: An alert adult on a sidewalk is having chest pain you suspect is a heart attack. According to AHA Part 10, what dose of aspirin is recommended if the person can chew and swallow it and has no contraindications?

answers.text: 5 to 10 mg of aspirin
5000 mg of aspirin
1000 mg of aspirin
162 to 325 mg of aspirin

explanations.a: 5 to 10 mg is far below the AHA-specified dose and would have no clinical effect.
explanations.b: 5000 mg is a toxic dose and far above the AHA recommendation.
explanations.c: 1000 mg exceeds the AHA-recommended dose without added benefit.
explanations.d: AHA Part 10 directs rescuers to encourage alert adults experiencing chest pain to chew and swallow aspirin in the 162 to 325 mg range, unless they have a known aspirin allergy or have been told not to take it.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: A person experiencing chest pain tells you they are allergic to aspirin. According to AHA Part 10, what action is appropriate?

answers.text: Give aspirin anyway because the benefit outweighs the risk
Give double the normal dose to overcome any allergic reaction
Withhold aspirin and wait for advanced care to arrive
Give a tablet of ibuprofen as a substitute

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 explicitly states aspirin should not be given if the person has a known aspirin allergy.
explanations.b: Doubling the dose worsens the allergic reaction risk and is not the AHA recommendation.
explanations.c: AHA Part 10 directs rescuers to withhold aspirin if the person has a known aspirin allergy or has been told not to take it; if uncertain, wait for advanced care to arrive.
explanations.d: Ibuprofen is not a substitute for aspirin in suspected heart attack and is not part of AHA BLS guidance.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 teaches the F.A.S.T. method to recognize the warning signs of stroke. What do the four letters represent?

answers.text: Fever, Aches, Sneezing, Tiredness
Fall, Aspirin, Sit, Treatment
Fast, Active, Strong, Talking
Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911

explanations.a: These are general symptoms of viral illness, not stroke.
explanations.b: These do not match the AHA F.A.S.T. acronym.
explanations.c: These do not match the AHA F.A.S.T. acronym.
explanations.d: AHA Part 10 says F.A.S.T. stands for Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call 911.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 describes stroke as a 'time-critical' emergency. Which statement best summarizes the rationale?

answers.text: Every minute counts because more brain tissue dies as treatment is delayed
Stroke patients can wait days for treatment without consequence
Strokes only matter if the person is over 80 years old
Stroke care does not depend on the time of symptom onset

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 says stroke is a time-critical emergency where every minute counts — every minute treatment is delayed, more brain tissue dies.
explanations.b: Days of delay would result in massive irreversible brain injury and death.
explanations.c: Stroke can occur at any adult age and treatment matters at all ages.
explanations.d: Time of symptom onset is one of the key factors guiding stroke treatment and triage decisions.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 describes how stroke patients should be transported by EMS. Which statement matches the manual's triage guidance?

answers.text: They should be triaged to the nearest appropriate facility for stroke care, which may include Comprehensive, Thrombectomy-Capable, Primary, or Acute Stroke Ready Hospitals
They should always be transported to the nearest hospital regardless of capabilities
They should be driven by family rather than EMS to save resources
They should be told to wait at home for symptoms to clear

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 says the patient should be triaged to the nearest appropriate facility for stroke care — choices may include Comprehensive Stroke Centers, Thrombectomy-Capable Stroke Centers, Primary Stroke Centers, or Acute Stroke Ready Hospitals.
explanations.b: Going to the nearest hospital without considering stroke capabilities can delay essential treatments like thrombectomy.
explanations.c: Family transport delays definitive care and is not part of the AHA stroke pathway.
explanations.d: Stroke is not a 'wait it out' condition; immediate evaluation is essential.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: After an apparently successful rescue from a near-drowning, the rescued person seems alert and asks to be allowed to leave. According to AHA Part 10, what is the recommended action?

answers.text: Discharge the person at the scene if they appear normal
Anyone who has experienced drowning should be transported by EMS to the ED for evaluation and monitoring, even those alert and seeming recovered
Transport only if the person needed full CPR
Provide aspirin and send the person home

explanations.a: Apparently normal status at the scene does not rule out delayed pulmonary or neurologic complications.
explanations.b: AHA Part 10 says anyone who has experienced drowning should be transported by EMS to the ED for evaluation and monitoring — including people who needed only breaths and those who are alert and seem to have recovered.
explanations.c: Transport is recommended even when only breaths were needed, not just when CPR was performed.
explanations.d: Aspirin is not a treatment for drowning; medical evaluation is the appropriate next step.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.keyword: no abdominal thrusts to remove water
questions.text: A bystander asks whether they should perform abdominal thrusts to expel water from the lungs of a drowning victim before starting CPR. According to AHA Part 10, what is the correct guidance?

answers.text: Yes — abdominal thrusts effectively remove water from the lungs
Do not use abdominal thrusts to try to remove water from the breathing passages — they are not recommended and can be dangerous
Use 10 abdominal thrusts before any breaths
Always invert the victim by the ankles to drain water

explanations.a: AHA explicitly excludes abdominal thrusts as a water-removal technique.
explanations.b: AHA Part 10 says do not use abdominal thrusts to try to remove water from the breathing passages — these actions are not recommended and can be dangerous.
explanations.c: Abdominal thrusts before breaths are not part of the drowning resuscitation sequence.
explanations.d: Inverting the victim wastes time and can cause aspiration of stomach contents.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 helps rescuers recognize anaphylaxis. Which feature of the systemic presentation does the manual highlight?

answers.text: Anaphylaxis affects only the skin
Two or more body systems are involved when anaphylaxis is occurring
Anaphylaxis affects only the digestive system
Anaphylaxis is limited to changes in heart rate alone

explanations.a: Skin signs alone are common in mild allergic reactions; anaphylaxis involves multiple body systems.
explanations.b: AHA Part 10 says in anaphylaxis, two or more body systems are involved.
explanations.c: Anaphylaxis is multi-system; isolated digestive involvement is not the AHA description.
explanations.d: Heart rate changes are part of the picture but not the sole feature; multiple systems are affected.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: A coworker with a known peanut allergy develops hives, wheezing, and dizziness after eating. They have an epinephrine autoinjector. AHA Part 10 specifies where the injection should be given. Which location matches?

answers.text: Directly into the chest muscles
In the side of the thigh, about halfway between the hip and the knee
Directly into a vein in the wrist
On the back of the neck near the spine

explanations.a: Chest injection is not the AHA-described location and risks injury to underlying structures.
explanations.b: AHA Part 10 specifies the epinephrine injection is given in the side of the thigh, about halfway between the hip and the knee, identified as the safest location.
explanations.c: Epinephrine autoinjectors deliver intramuscular doses; intravenous injection is not appropriate from an autoinjector.
explanations.d: Neck injection is not part of any anaphylaxis treatment guidance.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: When using an epinephrine autoinjector during anaphylaxis, AHA Part 10 addresses whether clothing must be removed first. Which statement matches?

answers.text: Epinephrine can be given on bare skin or through clothing
All clothing must be removed first or the injection will not work
Clothing must be cut open with sterile scissors first
The injection should be given over multiple layers of clothing for safety

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 explicitly states epinephrine can be given on bare skin or through clothing.
explanations.b: Removing clothing wastes time during a time-critical emergency.
explanations.c: Sterile preparation is not required for emergency epinephrine autoinjector use.
explanations.d: The autoinjector is designed for delivery through normal clothing — not heavy multiple layers, but ordinary fabric is fine.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: AHA Part 10 lists circulatory signs of severe allergic reaction. Which set of findings matches the manual's list of poor perfusion signs in anaphylaxis?

answers.text: Very fast heart rate, changes in skin color, cool skin, not alert, low blood pressure, and dizziness
Slow heart rate of 50 with warm pink skin
Normal vital signs and full alertness throughout
High blood pressure with elevated body temperature

explanations.a: AHA Part 10 lists very fast heart rate, changes in skin color, cool skin, not alert, low blood pressure, and dizziness as circulation findings of poor perfusion in anaphylaxis.
explanations.b: Slow heart rate with warm pink skin is reassuring rather than a sign of poor perfusion.
explanations.c: Normal vital signs and full alertness rule out severe poor perfusion.
explanations.d: High BP with fever is not the AHA-described shock pattern of anaphylaxis.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: After successful AED-assisted resuscitation of a pregnant person, ROSC is achieved. AHA Part 4 specifies a positioning recommendation post-revival. What is it?

answers.text: Place the person flat on their back with no positioning
Place the person face down to reduce reflux risk
Place the person on their left side to improve blood flow to their heart and to the fetus
Place the person sitting fully upright in a chair

explanations.a: Supine positioning allows the gravid uterus to compress major vessels and reduce blood return to the heart.
explanations.b: Prone positioning blocks the airway and is contraindicated.
explanations.c: AHA Part 4 says if the pregnant person is revived, place them on their left side to improve blood flow to the heart and therefore to the fetus.
explanations.d: Sitting fully upright is not the AHA-recommended post-resuscitation position for a pregnant person.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: After a long, unsuccessful resuscitation attempt, the team leader is reviewing AHA recovery and survivorship guidance with the rescuers. Which statement most accurately reflects that guidance?

answers.text: Recovery support is only relevant for the patient, never for rescuers
Rescuers and caregivers may benefit from psychological support, resiliency, burnout prevention, and effective debriefing after the event
Family members of survivors should not be involved in any recovery activities
Debriefing should be delayed at least 6 months after the event

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 extends recovery and survivorship considerations beyond the patient to caregivers and rescuers.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 explicitly notes rescuers and caregivers may benefit from psychological support, resiliency, burnout prevention, and effective debriefing.
explanations.c: Family members are part of the support network and AHA encourages a multimodal recovery approach.
explanations.d: Effective debriefing is recommended after the event, not delayed by months.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: A bystander finds an unresponsive adult with slow, shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils, and a needle nearby. According to AHA Part 9 opioid emergency response, what is the correct sequence?

answers.text: Wait until the person becomes pulseless before doing anything
Activate the emergency response system, begin standard BLS care (open airway, rescue breaths, compressions if pulseless), and give naloxone if available — even before confirming the substance
Administer naloxone and then leave to find more bystanders
Place in recovery position and assume sleep if breathing

explanations.a: Waiting for arrest worsens outcome; intervention starts at the first opioid emergency findings.
explanations.b: AHA Part 9: opioid emergency response combines standard BLS (airway, breathing, compressions) with naloxone administration if available and trained.
explanations.c: Naloxone is part of the response, not a substitute for BLS or for staying with the patient.
explanations.d: Slow shallow breathing in this scenario is not normal sleep; intervene.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.keyword: naloxone onset 2 to 3 minutes second dose
questions.text: A patient has been given intranasal naloxone for suspected opioid overdose. According to AHA Part 9, how soon should the rescuer expect a response?

answers.text: Within 5 seconds
After at least 30 minutes
Typically within 2–3 minutes; if no response, a second dose can be given and BLS care continues meanwhile
Naloxone never produces an observable change in response

explanations.a: 5 seconds is too fast; even IV naloxone takes longer.
explanations.b: 30 minutes is far longer than typical onset.
explanations.c: AHA Part 9: intranasal/IM naloxone onset is typically 2–3 minutes; if no response, repeat dose, continue BLS, and seek advanced care.
explanations.d: Naloxone reliably reverses opioid respiratory depression when sufficient dose reaches the brain.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.keyword: heart attack 911 aspirin rest CPR ready
questions.text: An adult complains of crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm with shortness of breath and diaphoresis. According to AHA Part 9, what is the correct lay-rescuer action?

answers.text: Call 911 immediately, have the person sit or lie comfortably, give chewable aspirin if they are not allergic and not contraindicated, and prepare to start CPR if they become unresponsive
Drive the person to the hospital yourself rather than calling 911
Give a large dose of acetaminophen for the chest pain
Tell the person to walk it off and continue normal activity

explanations.a: AHA Part 9: 911 first (EMS can begin treatment in route), have the person rest, aspirin if appropriate, monitor for arrest.
explanations.b: Driving private wastes EMS treatment time and is dangerous if cardiac arrest occurs en route.
explanations.c: Acetaminophen does not treat MI and is not part of the AHA recommendation.
explanations.d: Continued activity may extend infarction; rest reduces myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.keyword: stroke FAST BE-FAST 911 time of onset
questions.text: A bystander notices an adult suddenly has a drooping face on one side, slurred speech, and weakness in one arm. According to AHA Part 9, what is the correct response?

answers.text: Wait several hours to see if the symptoms resolve
Give the person aspirin and food before any other action
Drive the person to a clinic instead of an emergency department
Recognize the FAST/BE-FAST signs (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time), call 911 immediately, note the time of symptom onset, and tell EMS — early thrombolysis or thrombectomy depends on time

explanations.a: Stroke is time-critical; waiting reduces eligibility for thrombolytics and thrombectomy.
explanations.b: Aspirin is contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke and is not given by lay rescuers; food/drink risks aspiration.
explanations.c: A clinic typically lacks stroke imaging and treatment; EMS goes to a stroke-capable hospital.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9: BE-FAST/FAST recognition + 911 + record time of onset = the lay rescuer protocol for stroke.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: A drowning victim is pulled from the water unresponsive. According to AHA Part 10 drowning guidance, what is unique about the rescue protocol?

answers.text: Begin with rescue breaths before chest compressions when possible — drowning is primarily a hypoxic insult, so opening the airway and providing 2–5 initial breaths can address the underlying problem early in resuscitation
Skip rescue breaths entirely because the lungs are full of water
Compress only at half the standard depth because the chest is wet
Wait until the victim is fully dry before starting CPR

explanations.a: AHA Part 10: drowning is a hypoxic arrest; deliver rescue breaths first if trained and able, then proceed with standard CPR — this is one of the few situations where breaths-first sequence applies.
explanations.b: Lungs are not "full of water" in most drowning; airway intervention and ventilation are essential.
explanations.c: Compression depth is unchanged by wet skin.
explanations.d: Drying is not required; remove from water and begin BLS immediately.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: An adult eats peanuts and within minutes has facial swelling, hives, throat tightness, and wheezing. According to AHA Part 9, what is the priority intervention?

answers.text: Give an oral antihistamine and observe for 1 hour
Wait until cardiac arrest before giving epinephrine
Administer epinephrine via auto-injector intramuscularly into the lateral thigh, call 911, and prepare to give a second dose if symptoms persist or recur
Give cold water and chest compressions

explanations.a: Antihistamines do not reverse airway/cardiovascular collapse; epinephrine does.
explanations.b: Epinephrine should be given for anaphylaxis BEFORE arrest — early administration prevents arrest.
explanations.c: AHA Part 9 / general anaphylaxis guidelines: IM epinephrine into the lateral thigh (vastus lateralis) is first-line; 911 + monitor + repeat dose at 5–15 min if needed.
explanations.d: Cold water is not a treatment; CPR is for unresponsive arrest only.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: A bystander asks why epinephrine for anaphylaxis is given intramuscularly into the LATERAL THIGH rather than the arm. According to AHA / general anaphylaxis guidance, what is the rationale?

answers.text: Arm injection is not effective for any drug
IM injection into the vastus lateralis (lateral thigh) provides faster and higher peak plasma concentrations than the deltoid for epinephrine, with reliable absorption even in shock
Thigh injection avoids hitting any nerve
It is simply tradition with no physiologic basis

explanations.a: Many drugs are effective via the deltoid; the rationale here is specific to epinephrine pharmacokinetics in shock.
explanations.b: Anaphylaxis evidence shows lateral-thigh IM epinephrine produces higher and faster peak levels than deltoid IM, particularly in shock states with peripheral vasoconstriction.
explanations.c: Nerve avoidance is one consideration in any IM site, but the primary AHA rationale is pharmacokinetic.
explanations.d: There is a specific evidence-based reason: faster, higher, more reliable absorption.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.keyword: pregnancy cardiac arrest manual left uterine displacement
questions.text: A 32-week-pregnant woman is in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 9 pregnancy in cardiac arrest, what is the key modification to standard BLS?

answers.text: Skip compressions entirely
Compress at the upper sternum instead of the lower half
Defibrillation is contraindicated during pregnancy

Perform high-quality CPR with the patient supine, providing manual left uterine displacement (one-handed pull or two-handed push) to relieve aortocaval compression — this restores venous return that the gravid uterus would otherwise obstruct

explanations.a: Compressions remain essential; the modification is uterine displacement, not omitting compressions.
explanations.b: Compression position is unchanged — lower half of the sternum.
explanations.c: Defibrillation is safe and indicated for shockable rhythms in pregnancy.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9: manual left uterine displacement during CPR (continuous LUD by a dedicated person) relieves aortocaval compression and improves cardiac output and resuscitation success.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: During CPR on a pregnant patient with no ROSC after several minutes, AHA Part 9 includes what additional advanced consideration if the gestational age is sufficient and resources are available?

answers.text: Resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem cesarean delivery), ideally initiated within 4–5 minutes of arrest if no ROSC, to relieve aortocaval compression and potentially deliver a viable infant
Wait 30 minutes before considering any obstetric intervention
Hysterotomy is never indicated during cardiac arrest
Forgo all advanced interventions and focus on family notification

explanations.a: AHA Part 9: in a pregnant patient (typically ≥20 weeks gestation) who has not achieved ROSC, perimortem cesarean delivery is considered, ideally beginning at 4 minutes of arrest with delivery by 5 minutes — improves both maternal and fetal outcomes.
explanations.b: 30 minutes is far too long; the 4–5 minute target reflects the time pressure of cerebral and fetal ischemia.
explanations.c: Perimortem cesarean is an established advanced intervention in maternal cardiac arrest with sufficient gestational age.
explanations.d: Active advanced resuscitation including hysterotomy when indicated is the AHA recommendation.

questions.name: Special Situations and Recovery
questions.text: After participating in an unsuccessful resuscitation, a lay rescuer feels distressed and has trouble sleeping for several days. According to AHA recovery framework, what is the appropriate guidance?

answers.text: Suppress the feelings and continue normal activity without acknowledgment

Recognize that emotional reactions including grief, intrusive thoughts, and sleep disturbance are normal after a resuscitation event; seek peer support, professional counseling, or critical incident debriefing if symptoms persist
Avoid all CPR involvement permanently
Take prescription sleep medication without medical evaluation

explanations.a: Suppression often worsens long-term outcomes; AHA promotes acknowledgment.
explanations.b: AHA recovery framework: rescuer mental health is part of the response system; normalize reactions, encourage peer support and professional resources when needed.
explanations.c: Avoiding CPR permanently after a difficult call is not the AHA recommendation; mental health support and gradual reengagement are.
explanations.d: Self-medicating without evaluation is unsafe.
